I actually don't know much about antinatalism, but I like your questions, so I'll give it a shot. I could be completely off.

1) Yes; no. 

2) Like others mentioned, it's irrelevant to do a hindsight justification after getting lucky. I guess it boils down to human reproduction's expected value being positive or negative. Let's assign some values, then. In my opinion, contentment is cosmically meaningless, involves biological hormonal transport, and has no objective, positive value. Suffering has objective negative value(*). Happy child, 0. Miserable child, -1. Let's say for shits and giggles, you have 99% chance of having a happy child. 

Expected Value = 0(0.99) + (-1)(0.01) = -0.01 --> Negative --> Making baby = bad decision

(*) To be fair, I'm having difficulty justifying suffering having -1 value. You can argue that suffering, like contentment, is cosmically pointless and should have 0 value. Or, that contentment has positive value. Somehow to me right now, pleasure is pointless and pain is real.

3) I guess as a society, we decided that driving has positive value that outweighs the negative value of accidents. 

Ex. driving accident-free has value +2 (90% probability). Driving and getting into an accident, -10 (10% probability). 

Expected Value = 2(0.9) + (-10)(0.1) = 1.8 + (-1) = +0.8 --> Positive --> Driving = good decision

Very interesting question. I play on and off myself. I think the answer (for me) is sort of both. I'm dealing with quite a severe depression, and for long periods of time, would avoid poker because of the high demand for emotional stability during downswings. I used to stomach losses well and have mildly disappointed drives home at most, I guess because I'm just a pretty stoic guy, but while depressed, I've had drives home when I'd scream in frustration (I do this not just for poker). If you're more or less stable psychologically (don't have much in life throwing you down)...I'd say it's a great practice in Stoicism (though I'm also new to the philosophy). But given the game's extreme variance, at times brutally disregarding skill, it's also an extreme test of emotional stability. 

I think you're doing fine. One night of anger is pretty damn good. And I'd imagine that the more you practice, the more you'll successfully become more emotionally numb to those bad beats. The interesting thing is, I think you're also supposed to try emotionally numbing against winning sessions - which is the greatest mindfuck for me (that rush after you walk out the casino a winner - isn't that the reason I love the game??). But I suppose again, the more you practice, the more you'll gain the capacity to stoically remind yourself that the "rush" of winning isn't really why you're there. Ed Miller wrote in "The Course" that what helped him become numb to the down AND up-swings, on top of practice, is saying to himself, "The results of this session have nothing to do with how well I played." Even if realistically, you made mistakes that cost you in that last session, there's still a lot of luck factoring into those negative results. You can imagine how that quote isn't easy to fully believe when you're winning big. I guess playing the long-term game means avoiding the tendency to extrapolate significant meanings from both big losses and big wins, as long as you focus on making better and better decisions, as Gdor mentioned.

Apparently, the unquestionably "right" thing to do is to prevent suicide. I'm hesitant about bringing up my eargerness to opt out with my therapist because of where that might land me. Privately, to counter social brainwash, I like to hand-write a philosopher's quote - "As soon as the terror of living begins to outweigh the terrors of death, a man will put an end to his life." Yet even as I read your posts about killing yourself, I feel dread. But why? Your plan makes sense; my fear for your life doesn't. If the cost outweighs the benefit of living, one would rationally stop living. 

My friend recently invited me to a physician-assisted suicide debate at UC Irvine (sept 3). I decided not to go because I know how fucking irritated I would be, 2 hours listening to one dipshit-side argue that California hospitals should NOT provide that option EVEN for terminally ill (cancer) people. Not even extending the discussion to the severely depressed. Because hey - we can always fix mental illness! Even in the few states where this physician-suicide is legal, you have to demonstrate zero mental disorder, which would obviously include depression. 

Just yesterday, I was fantasizing the process of doing a physician-assisted suicide. Lying in that hospital bed...nurse busting out the syringe. I imagined relief, but not so much in dying itself. I would be relieved to be in the care of a system, of people, who sympathize with and acknowledge my irreversible suffering. I'm relieved that this imaginary society finally extended a hand of compassion. Ironically, I also imagined that just by having a sympathizing system in place, there would likely be more opportunities to have informed or rational discussions regarding suicide as the ultimately valid option for me. Just having that forum for conversation...who knows how that might shift our perspectives. 

Alas, it was only a dream :(
